newsitem.title: JAPAN: SAfrican investment ceiling seen above 160,000 rand.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican investment ceiling seen above 160,000 rand.

text.p: South Africa's Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Wednesday it was unlikely that South Africa's ceiling for individual investment abroad would be set below 160,000 rand ($35,570).

Manuel told reporters the country's travel allowance had been raised to 80,000 rand per person per year, and referring to the investment limit, he said: "It is unlikely it will be set less than what a couple will take out."

"These figures are not being fixed yet. The announcement will be made by the Reserve Bank probably within the next week or so," said the minister, who arrived here on Sunday for a four-day visit to promote South African government bonds.
Johannesburg plans to relax foreign exchange controls next month to allow ordinary South Africans to invest in offshore markets up to a certain limit.
The move triggered worries of a possible capital flight, putting pressure on the rand over the last few days.
But Manuel said he was not worried about the recent fall in the rand's value.
"The sky has not fallen because there has been a little bit of movement of the rand," he said.
On Monday, the rand hit its latest low of 4.5040 to the dollar, the dollar's first move above 4.50 rand in four months.

Asked about the size of the possible outflow of individual capital, Manuel said: "Your guess is as good as mine... Chances are that there are a number of South Africans who already have wealth abroad. It's hard to speculate."
Manuel also said South African interest rates might be lowered later this year. The country's Reserve Bank governor, Chris Stals, hinted at such a move in Switzerland last weekend.
"Indications are positive for some reduction in interest rates later this year," Manuel said.
Asked about gross domestic product (GDP) growth, he said: "We still believe the country is on track for 2.5 percent growth this year."

South Africa's GDP showed a surprise fall of 1.0 percent in the first quarter from the previous quarter -- the first contraction since the first quarter of 1994 -- mainly due to a decline in agricultural production.
Manuel would not comment on the response to South Africa's 40 billion yen ($360 million) seven-year yen samurai bond. Its subscription period expires on Friday.
He also declined to give any details of a Yankee bond which is expected to be issued next month.
He said South Africa was given a rating by Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Co of the United States earlier on Wednesday that should allow Johannesburg access to a wider range of investors.
"We can access a wider array of capital sources in the United States, and we think this is good for South Africa's future Yankees," he said.

Maria Ramos, South African director-general of finance, said last month that the samurai and Yankee issues together should raise four billion rand ($803 million) this year as outlined in the country's 1997/98 budget. ($1=4.498 rand) ($1=111 yen)
